question: to the Commission Wouter Beke (PPE) Subject:

Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 on nature restoration (the Nature Restoration Regulation), Member States must submit their draft national restoration plans to the Commission by 1 September 2026 at the latest. These plans may have significant implications for the granting of permits, as well as for agriculture, infrastructure, businesses and investment. At the same time, there is still insufficient clarity regarding the funding of the measures required to achieve the regulation’s objectives, which will come in addition to existing instruments such as the CAP. Moreover, various simplification processes are underway in the context of EU environmental policy, which include the stress test under the Birds and Habitats Directives. Given that the Nature Restoration Regulation builds on the Habitats Directive, legal certainty for Member States, citizens and businesses is essential. 1.
Does the Commission recognise that national restoration plans may have significant implications for the granting of permits, for businesses and for investment in the Member States?
Is the Commission prepared to consider postponing the submission of national restoration plans?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (2.9.2026) The Commission recognises that the preparation and implementation of national restoration plans (NRP) may have practical implications in Member States, including for land-use choices, sectoral planning and, depending on national implementation, for permitting processes, businesses and investment. However, the Nature Restoration Regulation (NRR)1 does not create a new permitting regime. It leaves to Member States to align the implementation of the Regulation with existing frameworks, including the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive2 and the Birds and Habitats Directives3, as well as with existing national tools and procedures, including permitting. The NRR also requires Member States to involve stakeholders in NRP preparation, to ensure it fits local circumstances and to support affected stakeholders if relevant. This should allow Member States to integrate restoration obligations in a coherent manner while reducing administrative burden. The NRR provides for a stepwise process. After submission of a draft NRP by 1 September 2026, the subsequent assessment of the draft by the Commission4 and its observations are intended to support a constructive dialogue with Member States and may lead to further refinements of the NRP before its finalisation by September 2027. NRPs may also be reviewed thereafter5. In this context, the Commission does not intend to extend the deadline for submitting draft NRP but will continue to support Member States in finalising and implementing them as committed in its communication Simplifying for sustainable competitiveness6. Nature restoration is an urgent but continuous process thus it is in the interest of the resilience and competitiveness of the EU not to delay it further.
1 Regulation (EU) 2024/1991 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 June 2024 on nature

restoration and amending Regulation (EU) 2022/869, OJ L, 2024/1991, 29.7.2024. 2 Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 December 2011 on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2012, p. 1–21, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council of 16 April 2014, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014, p. 1–18. 3 Directive 2009/147/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 30 November 2009 on the conservation of wild birds, OJ L 20, 26.1.2010, p. 7–25.; and Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7–50. 4 In accordance with Article 17 of the Nature Restoration Regulation. 5 In accordance with Article 19 of the Nature Restoration Regulation. 6 https://environment.ec.europa.eu/publications/simplification-administrative-burdens-environmentallegislation_en.
